1:
Keil and Delitzsch open with the placing of the whole section. The words of God that follow contain no chronological data, but their contents connect them closely with the foregoing announcements of judgment, which makes it probable they fell within the eleven months between two dated visions; their purpose is to show the worthlessness of the false confidence on which the impenitent rested, and to affirm the certainty of the predicted destruction, in the hope of awakening a hardened generation to the repentance without which peace could never be enjoyed. Clarke summarises the chapter as showing those already in captivity that their brethren left behind would be in a much worse condition than they.

Henry begins with what did not happen. The prophet may have hoped, after the vision of the glory went up from him, to see it a third time; but he never saw it again, and yet the word of the Lord came to him, God having spoken to the fathers in divers manners, so that men heard his words without seeing visions. Faith comes by hearing that word of prophecy which is more sure than vision, and we may keep up our communion with God without raptures and ecstasies. He then explains why the sign was needed: as long as the king was on the throne the captives flattered themselves that he would make his part good against Babylon, and he may have privately sent them encouragement, so that while they were fed with these vain hopes they could neither submit to their affliction nor get good by it.

The rebellious house is described the same way by all. Ellicott takes the not seeing and not hearing for that perverse refusal so often spoken of in scripture, and says it was because of this disposition that a sign was given which they could not shut their eyes to. Clarke presses the point morally: it is not want of grace that destroys them, for they have eyes and will not use them, and no man is lost because he had insufficient grace but because he abused what he had. Wesley says they have capacity to understand if they would. Gill describes them as murmuring and repenting that they had surrendered.

Calvin asks why God warned the prophet of their obstinacy before commanding him. It was to give him fortitude, lest seeing his labour consumed in vain he should withdraw; for it is a severe temptation to the servants of God to speak to the deaf and have their doctrine not merely rejected but refused with ignominy, so that they think silence better, since where the word is so despised it only exposes the name of God to reproach. He adds a second reason: the prophet might object that it would be ridiculous to take up staff and scrip and hat like a traveller, and the Israelites no doubt derided the performance as a boyish amusement, so God gives him the reason of the plan beforehand. Calvin compares an old legal fiction described by a Roman writer, in which men disputing a field went through an imaginary going out to view it rather than trouble the judge to ride over the ground.

On the stuff itself Ellicott adds precision. The phrase is elsewhere rendered furnish thyself to go into captivity, and the word covers everything an emigrant would need; the removing is the same word rendered captivity in the next verse. He reconstructs the action: the preparations are made and the goods carried out during the day but the prophet himself does not go out until evening, as one who must abandon his home uses the whole day to carry out all he can and then leaves when the day is done. Gill and Calvin both list what such a traveller takes, and Calvin notes that the Latins called garments as well as other goods vessels.
4:
The digging is the sharpest of the signs. Ellicott supplies the material fact, that the wall was probably of sun-dried brick, the common building material, so there was no great difficulty in getting through it, but that entering a house this way indicates stealth and secrecy; the goods were to go out openly through the door by day, and then the prophet was to re-enter at evening and carry out secretly what he would not otherwise be allowed to take. Gill and Clarke both refer the sign to the escape of the king, who went out by night through a breach. Wesley has him avoid the door as one who knows there is a guard on it, and dig at some back part of the house himself, either for haste or for secrecy. Calvin makes the point general: there would be no free egress, so that no safety remained but in concealed flight, the Jews escaping through their hiding-place as thieves do by digging through a wall.

The covered face divides them. Ellicott allows that it might primarily be a token of grief, but insists the whole action is distinctly prophetic and this sign especially so, and points to the capture of the king, who escaped by night, was pursued and taken, had his eyes put out and was carried in chains. Clarke goes further with a conjecture: the covering of the face might mean that the king was carried to Babylon on the shoulders of men in a kind of palanquin with a cloth tied over his eyes because of the recent wounds. Gill reports that two ancient versions turn the clause round, so that the prophet himself is carried on the shoulders of another, and prefers the plainer sense. Ellicott also removes two supplied pronouns and renders the word for twilight, used only three times, as dark.

The obedience is noticed by both the voices that dwell on it. Gill says the thing might seem ridiculous and the prophet be bantered and despised for it, yet being the will of God he was obedient, as the servants of the Lord should be even in things for which they may be laughed at. Calvin makes the same point sharper: nothing is more distasteful to ingenuous natures than to provoke the laughter of all men, and the prophet knew the action would be exposed to jeers and reproaches, yet he esteemed nothing of equal moment with pleasing God.

The question the people ask is where Calvin and Ellicott diverge. Ellicott takes the morning message as implying that the action was actually performed, since the divine word comes in answer to their inquiry. Calvin reads the inquiry itself as derision, and argues from the text: those who suppose the Israelites asked in genuine ignorance do not sufficiently consider the words, since the epithet rebellious is not repeated in vain, and had the question proceeded from mere folly God would not have called them so. They jeered at what seemed to them trifling, having found a plausible ground for it in a spectacle that looked childish; but God does not suffer his servants to be reviled so, and since the prophet bore the marks of his office the people ought to have inquired modestly, for whatever we know to flow from God should be received reverently without controversy, and where there is obscurity docility ought to precede the question. Clarke and Wesley both take the burden as the prediction concerning the prince, a burden the kingdom shall groan under, and Ellicott notes that although it was directed to the king and his princes the people were necessarily involved.
12:
Ellicott handles a small historical difficulty at the outset. The digging through the wall is not mentioned in the account of the flight of the king, yet it need not be taken figuratively, since a breach at a place unwatched by the enemy might easily be arranged for secrecy and as easily passed over in a brief narrative. The covered face he takes as a natural means of avoiding recognition, though also an intimation of what the next verse hints more plainly. Wesley has the king disguised as a servant and choosing the twilight as the time that best favours his design. Calvin explains why the king alone is named, since it was almost incredible that the enemy could not be appeased, surrender often preserving even kings after they have been led in triumph.

The net is read two ways. Clarke finds in it an ancient manner of fighting: one combatant carried a small casting net, and if he could throw it over the head of his antagonist he despatched him with the sword, while if he missed he had to run and readjust it, pursued all the while by the other, so that the one was called the netman and the other the pursuer. Gill takes the net simply for the Chaldean army raised up and brought against him. Calvin takes the figure as God claiming for himself what the Chaldeans executed: they laid their snares when advised of the flight and knew its direction, yet the whole affair was under the government of heaven, and unless God had provided for the event all their endeavours would have proved fruitless.

That he should be brought to Babylon and not see it is explained by both the voices that notice it. Clarke says his eyes were put out before he went, so that he was carried thither blind and died there. Ellicott gives the same solution, that the prophet does not explain how it could be but another prophet makes it plain, and adds a curious story from a historian: the king was inclined to believe the warning that he should be carried captive, but when this prophecy came saying he should not see the land he thought the two contradictory and so disbelieved them both.

The scattering and the remnant close the entry. Ellicott notes that the people were not carried to Babylon only but scattered wherever they could find refuge, the last remnant escaping into Egypt after the murder of the governor. Calvin argues against a common reading of the survivors: some think God speaks here of the faithful whom he preserved in the midst of death, and there is indeed some mitigation, but it does not suit the passage, which speaks of the people in general; the promise was not directed peculiarly to the elect but shows that exile would not be the end of their woes, and that the survivors were left not because God was reconciled but that their crimes might be spread among the nations. When they are said to declare their abominations he does not mean the confession that is a sign of repentance but a speech made by the fact itself, the exile proclaiming aloud that these men were abandoned. Ellicott takes the declaring both ways, by word of mouth and by conduct, and its purpose as removing the impression among the heathen that God was unable to protect his people; he also notes a play on words in the original, the men of number being men who can be counted and the declaring something like a recounting. Wesley draws the happiest conclusion of any of them, that the dispersion of sinners who had done God much dishonour in their own country proves the dispersion of penitents who shall do him much service in other countries.
17:
A second sign follows. Gill sets the two side by side: the former signified their going into captivity, this their famine and distress at the siege. Ellicott calls it another symbolical action, and Clarke has the prophet assume the manner of a person every moment afraid of his life, with nothing but a morsel of bread and a little water. Gill glosses the quaking as the bearing of one in surprise, or one who has got an ague upon him. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the carrying out of the sign is nowhere recorded, not because it is doubtful but simply taken for granted, and that the trouble could only be expressed by gesture; they also warn against reading too much into the elements, since bread and water is the standing expression for food, so scanty provision is not to be sought in the words.

Henry presses the cost to the prophet. Though under no apprehension of danger to himself and living in plenty, he must eat his bread with quaking and drink his water with trembling; and this was no pretence, but a man who believed the judgment, was far from desiring it, and was affected with grief at the prospect. From this he draws a rule: those who speak of the ruin coming upon impenitent sinners must speak feelingly, as men that know the terrors of the Lord, and be content to endure hardness so that they may do good. Calvin explains why a sign was needed, since simple and unadorned teaching would not have been effective among such hearers; the prophet is made the image of the besieged people, that the spectacle might the more affect slow and slothful men.

Calvin fills in the fear itself. The Jews thought their garrison made them impregnable, and the Lord had often to remove that trust; a besieged city always fears for itself, and the enemy so harasses it that fatigue at length compels surrender. Henry gives two causes of the care: either they feared the provisions would not hold out, or they were continually expecting the alarms of the enemy, their life hanging in doubt before them.

Who the people of the land are is disputed. Gill takes them for the Israelites captive in Chaldea, ready to murmur at their own case as miserable and at that of the Jews at Jerusalem as happy, and here taught that they were mistaken; Calvin likewise reads it of the ten tribes, and adds that their outcry was against God and his servants, especially Jeremiah. Ellicott agrees the address is to the fellow captives, and notes that these prophecies, though they concern Jerusalem, were taught primarily to the exiles; he cites Jerome for the suggestion that the prophecies of Ezekiel were sent to Jerusalem while the utterances made there were sent into Chaldea. Wesley divides the phrase, taking the people for the fellow captives but the land for the countries round about Jerusalem, and reads the violence as the injustice, oppression and tyranny of the Jews toward one another. Ellicott, following the margin, reads the stripping as the land losing all that makes it desirable.

The last verse widens the ruin. Gill notes that not Jerusalem only but the other cities of Judea, then full of inhabitants, were laid waste by the Chaldeans. Calvin adds that no single corner might suppose itself free, since Jerusalem was the head of the nation and after its fall the rest were easily overthrown. On the closing formula he observes that they had heard this from the prophets from earliest childhood, God having borne witness by the frequent succours which snatched that wretched people from death; but their impiety had so stupified them that they despised both teaching and open judgments. Those who closed their ears when he invited them as servants must at last feel him to be God when he is silent and executing.
21:
The chapter turns from sign to saying. Gill notes that after the two signs they hardened themselves against the things signified, because the time of accomplishment was not yet. Henry sets out the strategy: various methods had been used to awaken this secure and careless people, the prophecies confirmed by visions and illustrated by signs with such power that one would think they must needs be wrought upon; but they evaded conviction by telling themselves that the judgments, if they came at all, would not come of a long time. He draws out what lay under the proverb: the judgments had not come when expected, therefore some visions had failed, therefore all would, and they would never trust a prophet again, having been more frightened than hurt.

Calvin reads the saying as ridicule. The long threatening of the prophets, so far from leading to repentance, had made the people more obstinate and callous. It was monstrous, he says, that a people who had imbibed the law and the prophets from childhood should break forth against God as if he had spoken falsely; from the delay they argued that they had no cause for fear, since whatever Jeremiah and the rest predicted had passed away. So unbelievers turn the patience of God into material for obduracy: he spares them and invites them to repentance, and they count the days and years, and when judgment is not executed at once they esteem the words of the prophet as idle fables. When God is supposed false in both promise and threatening, all religion is abolished.

The others fill in the saying and its speakers. Gill takes the question as put not in ignorance but in indignation at the boldness of those who used it. Clarke assigns it to scoffers who, because vengeance was not speedily executed on an evil work, set their heart to do iniquity, reasoning that the predictions will either not come in their days or wholly fail; and he marvels that the means used by a gracious God to bring sinners to repentance should be made the instruments of their destruction. Wesley glosses it as a short saying commonly used, that the days of wrath are a great while hence and the visions with which Jeremiah and Ezekiel would fright them come to nothing. Ellicott adds a distinction: the land of Israel here is not the same as in Israel in the next verse, but points to a proverb current among those not yet carried into captivity, who fancied they should not be. Clarke sets the reply against it: far from failing, time is posting on and the destruction threatened is at the door.

Two further confidences fall. Gill and Calvin agree on the false prophets, Gill describing the vain visions they had given out, that the people should be in peace and not delivered to the king of Babylon, and Calvin the flatterers who said God would not be so severe and that the predicted ruin of the city and temple was at variance with many promises; the true prophets were despised both by the contumacy of the people and by the acts of the false. Their mouth was stopped, not their persons removed, when the event proved their wickedness. On the last verse Calvin insists that the word of God is not to be separated from its effect, since he who speaks is not divided against himself, and whenever he opens his mouth he stretches out his hand to fulfil it; because the word seems cold and dissipated into air, the hand must always be considered. He explains the nearness as spoken after the manner of men, since a thousand years are with God as one day, yet those then alive would see it. Wesley reads the speaking more widely, of a succession of ministers to the end of the world, God never leaving himself without witness.
26:
The message is given twice. Gill reads the repetition as confirmation of what was before spoken, that they might assure themselves of a certain and speedy accomplishment of what the Lord had said by his prophet, and Clarke presses the promise home on the scoffers themselves: even these mockers shall live to see and feel this desolation.

Calvin distinguishes this second saying carefully from the first. What is condemned here is not the detestable blasphemy lately heard but oblique ridicule, whose tendency was first to weaken all confidence in prophecy and then to get rid of all heavenly doctrine. These men did not dare to bluster against God with swollen cheeks; where others concluded the prophecies vain because the time was put off, they granted that it might happen that God would accomplish what he had denounced by his servant, and added that meanwhile they would feast securely, since they would be dead before these things could happen. So there were two classes of men: some who utterly rejected the prophets and wantonly derided their threats, and others who neither openly nor distinctly pronounced God a liar but put far away from them the performance of what was announced. The first were so abandoned that they all but openly derided God, turning away all fear from their own feelings because he had prorogued the time.

He sets the two prophets side by side. Jeremiah had spent his strength in vain for many years, daily summoning them by a loud trumpet to the tribunal of God and setting the Chaldeans before their eyes; since he effected nothing, Ezekiel is chosen, and having inveighed against the fouler impudence he now attacks the hypocrite who had not yet gone so far as to vilify God by the use of words. The distinction does not make the second class safe, for the gliding down from such security to open contempt is easy: those who feign themselves quiet and without danger, because God patiently delays his judgments, at length determine that he is content with his own ease and does not regard human affairs. Hence the warning against the snares of Satan, and the counsel that we should not only abhor the foul blasphemy but, as soon as God threatens, go to meet his judgment rather than promise ourselves a long period of escape, which may render us so stupid as to deprive us of all fear.

Two smaller points close the chapter. Gill is undecided who the house of Israel here are, either those of the ten tribes in Babylon or the Jews in Judea, who were Israelites too; the prophet is directed to take notice of what they said and be a witness of it, since as a prophet he was himself concerned in it. On the final promise Calvin records another construction, which changes the number and resolves the clause as though each of the words severally should not be put off, but he judges the plainer reading to suit the context better, and returns to what he had said before, that it belongs to men to lie and to utter vainly what they cannot perform, while nothing of the kind ought to be imagined of God, whose hand is always in union with his speech. Clarke ends where the chapter ends: he had waited to be gracious, they abused his mercy, and at last the protracted wrath rushed upon them with irresistible force. Gill adds only that the message must be carried whether they will hear it or not.
